newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss central bank says small investors drove up its shares.
newsitem.headline: Swiss central bank says small investors drove up its shares.

text.p: Most investors who drove Swiss National Bank shares to record high levels in May were small private buyers rather than professionals, SNB board member Bruno Gehrig told a Swiss weekly newspaper.

A 400 percent jump between January and early May in the central bank's normally stodgy shares, spurred by plans to revalue and partly sell SNB gold reserves, has been one of the oddest twists of a bullish year on the Swiss stock market.
Gehrig told the paper Die Weltwoche that the central bank knew who bought its stock because they were registered shares.
"These are mainly smaller shareholders and private persons, not professional investors," Gehrig said without elaborating.

Unusually for central banks, the SNB is structured as a joint stock company with about 35 percent of its 100,000 shares in public hands. The rest is held by Swiss cantons, cantonal banks and other public institutions.

Despite the fact that dividends are strictly capped by law, SNB shares began moving up in March and shot to a peak of 3,000 Swiss francs on May 6, 400 percent above levels around 600 Swiss francs at the start of the year.
They have since settled back into a band around 2,000 Swiss francs and closed on Thursday at 1,985.
The central bank has said repeatedly it saw no reason for the sharp price gains and pinned the movement on speculation and a thin supply of tradeable shares.

Analysts and traders said buyers were speculating on a higher return to investors from a proposed revaluation of SNB gold reserves in line with market values. That would add some 14 billion Swiss francs to their book value.
The gains started after the government in March proposed revaluing reserves and using half the gains to fund a new Solidarity Foundation helping victims of poverty, disasters and human rights abuses.
